title: Seattle city leaders honor 9/11 victims, first responders on 25th anniversary
text:
Seattle firefighters, police, and city leaders held a remembrance ceremony Friday to honor the victims of the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks. They paid their respects to those who died and called for justice for survivors.

Chris Lombard saw the immediate aftermath of the 9/11 attacks up close.

On the morning of Sept. 11, Lombard was just getting off his shift for the  Washington Task Force 1, one of the 28 FEMA Urban Search and Rescue teams in the nation.

“ We all got the notice that morning that we were all getting ready to deploy, to go to either the Pentagon or New York,” Lombard told KUOW.

Lombard, now an assistant chief with the Seattle Fire Department, was sent to Ground Zero in New York to help with recovery at the massive pile of debris, concrete, and twisted steel.

“ Still to this day, I've never seen anything like it,” he said, “the damage, the carnage, and everything.”

He worked there for 10 days and said he was most impressed by the number of first responders working around the clock.

“Everybody was trying to rally. There were so many volunteers in New York trying to help in any and every way that they could,” Lombard said, “really a moving experience.”

Lombard is one of two people, along with  Battalion Chief Tom Richardson, still working at the Seattle Fire Department who went to Ground Zero shortly after the attacks. On Friday, Seattle Center hosted the fire department, Seattle Police, and Mayor Katie Wilson for a 25th anniversary ceremony.

Wilson called 9/11 “ a day forever scarred in the memory of those of us who lived through it.”

“It was a day that fundamentally altered the trajectory of our nation, that challenged our sense of self and our place in the world as nearly 3,000 people died due to the terrorist attacks that day,” she said.

Wilson recalled being 19 years old on the day of the attacks and watching the tragedy unfold on television with her parents. Wilson said she remembers how communities rallied together in the days following the attacks.

“ I also remember how solidarity with neighbors turned to fear, the Islamophobia that took root and made so many of our neighbors innocent targets of hatred and discrimination,” she said. Wilson also mentioned the long wars in Afghanistan and Iraq after 9/11 and “the toll they took on the Americans who fought in them, and on the people of other nations, and the profoundly changed world we live in today.”

Seattle Interim Police Chief Andre Sayles said watching the attacks led him to pursue his career in law enforcement.

“ Like every American, I was scared, stunned, and just couldn't process it,” Sayles said, “but in that time of darkness, I went back to understanding that I had a calling, and that calling was to be a police officer.”

Some leaders took the opportunity to call attention to the chronic health issues that have befallen 9/11 first responders.

Seattle Police Chaplain Charlie Scoma said the 2001 attacks still affect thousands of survivors today.

Scoma commended the heroism of people first on the scene “that day and throughout the last 25 years of fighting for others and for their health and for the benefits and things that our first responders and others need still this day.”

Seattle Fire Chief Harold Scoggins commended Lombard and Richardson for their service 25 years ago, as well as all of the people who worked to save lives. “ Residents and other first responders who came from outside of New York City to help have also died of cancer and all those other related illnesses after 9/11,” he said.

On Friday morning, firefighters at all 33 Seattle firehouses gathered for a moment of silence, and read aloud the names of the 343 firefighters who died during the attacks.

Two Seattle firetrucks hoisted a huge American flag in front of International Fountain in Seattle Center on Friday. Another flag atop the Space Needle flew at half-staff. The Seattle Firefighters Pipes and Drums band performed two songs on percussion and bagpipes, including a solemn version of “Amazing Grace.”

Lombard said after watching the U.S. come together 25 years ago, after watching people rally together, he wishes the country could rekindle that same level of unity.

“ We talk about never forgetting, but it's sad. I think there are a lot of people that are starting to forget that we are still just one big country, and being able to look across party lines and be able to see each other for the humanity that we are,” he said. “I hope it doesn't take another tragedy like that to unify us again as a country.”
